Create an undirected overlapping stochastic blockmodel object

Source: R/undirected_overlapping_sbm.R
overlapping_sbm.Rd

To specify an overlapping stochastic blockmodel, you must specify the number of nodes (via n), the mixing matrix (via k or B), and the block membership probabilities (optional, via pi). In an overlapping stochastic blockmodel, each node can belong to any number of blocks: zero, one, or several. We provide defaults for most of these options to enable rapid exploration, or you can invest the effort for more control over the model parameters. We strongly recommend setting the expected_degree or expected_density argument to avoid large memory allocations associated with sampling large, dense graphs.

Usage

overlapping_sbm(
  n,
  k = NULL,
  B = NULL,
  ...,
  pi = rep(1/k, k),
  sort_nodes = TRUE,
  force_pure = TRUE,
  poisson_edges = TRUE,
  allow_self_loops = TRUE
)

Arguments

n

The number of nodes in the overlapping SBM. Must be at least k when force_pure = TRUE.

k

(mixing matrix) The number of blocks in the blockmodel. Use when you don't want to specify the mixing-matrix by hand. When k is specified, B is set to a diagonally dominant matrix with value 0.8 along the diagonal and 0.1 / (k - 1) on the off-diagonal. This is subject to change, and may not be reproducible. k defaults to NULL. You must specify either k or B, but not both.

B

(mixing matrix) A k by k matrix of baseline connection intensities between blocks. Before any rescaling via expected_degree or expected_density, B[a, b] is the expected number of edges contributed to the pair of nodes \((i, j)\) by node \(i\)'s membership in block a and node \(j\)'s membership in block b. These contributions add up over all pairs of blocks that i and j belong to (see "Edge formulation" below). All elements of B must be contained in \([0, 1]\). matrix and Matrix objects are both acceptable. If B is not symmetric, it will be symmetrized via the update B := (B + t(B)) / 2, and the symmetrized B must be invertible. Defaults to NULL. You must specify either k or B, but not both.

...

Arguments passed on to undirected_factor_model

expected_degree

If specified, the desired expected degree of the graph. Specifying expected_degree simply rescales S to achieve this. Defaults to NULL. Do not specify both expected_degree and expected_density at the same time.

expected_density

If specified, the desired expected density of the graph. Specifying expected_density simply rescales S to achieve this. Defaults to NULL. Do not specify both expected_degree and expected_density at the same time.

pi

(block membership probabilities) A vector of length k whose jth element is the probability that a node belongs to block j. All elements must be contained in \([0, 1]\). Each node joins each block independently, so pi is not normalized and does not need to sum to one: sum(pi) is the expected number of blocks a node joins before nodes in no block are reassigned (ignoring force_pure). A node that joins no block is instead assigned to exactly one block, chosen with probability proportional to pi, so every node belongs to at least one block and at least one element of pi must be positive. Defaults to rep(1 / k, k), in which case a fraction of roughly \((1 - 1/k)^k \approx e^{-1}\) of nodes initially join no block and are reassigned to a single block chosen uniformly at random. Regardless of sort_nodes, pi is sorted in increasing order, and the rows and columns of B are permuted to match the new order of pi.

sort_nodes

Logical indicating whether or not to sort the nodes so that they are grouped by block. Useful for plotting. Defaults to TRUE. When TRUE, the rows of Z are sorted in decreasing lexicographic order, so that members of the first block come first, and within the members of the first block, members of the second block come first, and so on.

force_pure

Logical indicating whether or not to force presence of "pure nodes" (nodes that belong only to a single block) for the sake of identifiability. To include pure nodes, block membership sampling first proceeds as per usual. Then, after it is complete, k distinct nodes are chosen uniformly at random, and the memberships of the jth chosen node are overwritten so that it belongs to block j and to no other block. Requires n >= k. Defaults to TRUE.

poisson_edges

Logical indicating whether or not multiple edges are allowed to form between a pair of nodes. Defaults to TRUE. When FALSE, sampling proceeds as usual, and duplicate edges are removed afterwards. Further, when FALSE, we assume that S specifies a desired Bernoulli edge probability, and back-transform S to a Poisson parameterization before sampling (see "Edge formulation" below), so all elements of S (after symmetrizing and any rescaling) must be at most 1.

allow_self_loops

Logical indicating whether or not nodes should be allowed to form edges with themselves. Defaults to TRUE. When FALSE, sampling proceeds allowing self-loops, and these are then removed after the fact.

Value

An undirected_overlapping_sbm S3 object, a subclass of the undirected_factor_model() with the following additional fields:

  • Z: The block memberships of each node, as an n by k binary Matrix::Matrix(). Z[i, j] is one if node i belongs to block j and zero otherwise. Rows can contain any number of ones, including none. Columns are ordered to match pi and B. For this model, Z is identical to the latent positions X.

  • pi: Block membership probabilities for each block, sorted in increasing order.

  • B: The mixing matrix, as specified by the user (or the default when only k is given), with rows and columns permuted to match the order of pi. Note that B is not symmetrized or rescaled: the symmetrized and rescaled matrix used for sampling is S.

  • sorted: Logical indicating whether nodes are arranged by block membership (see sort_nodes).

Generative Model

overlapping_sbm() implements the stochastic blockmodel with overlaps (SBMO) of Kaufmann, Bonald and Lelarge (2016), with Poisson rather than Bernoulli edges. There are two levels of randomness in an overlapping stochastic blockmodel. First, for each node, we independently determine if that node is a member of each block. This is handled by overlapping_sbm(). Then, given these block memberships, we randomly sample edges between nodes. This second operation is handled by sample_edgelist(), sample_sparse(), sample_igraph() and sample_tidygraph(), depending on your desired graph representation.

Block memberships

Let \(Z \in \{0, 1\}^{n \times k}\) be the binary block membership matrix, and let \(z_i\) be its \(i\)th row, so that \(Z_{ia} = 1\) when node \(i\) belongs to block \(a\). Each entry is sampled independently as

$$ Z_{ia} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi_a), \qquad i = 1, \dots, n, \quad a = 1, \dots, k. $$

Unlike in dcsbm(), where each node belongs to exactly one block, or in mmsbm(), where each node splits one unit of membership among blocks, here a node can be a full member of several blocks at once.

Every node must belong to at least one block. After the Bernoulli draws above, any node with \(Z_{ia} = 0\) for every block \(a\) is assigned to exactly one block, chosen at random with probability \(\pi_a / \sum_b \pi_b\). As a result, the entries of \(Z\) are not exactly independent, and nodes that belong to a single block are somewhat more common than independent Bernoulli draws alone would give. When force_pure = TRUE, k randomly chosen nodes are then made pure members of one block each (see "Identifiability").

Degree heterogeneity

The overlapping SBM has no degree heterogeneity parameters (equivalently, \(\theta_i = 1\) for every node). Nodes that belong to more blocks tend to have higher expected degree, but all members of the same set of blocks have the same expected degree. See dcsbm() and mmsbm() for models with degree heterogeneity.

Edge formulation

Once we know the block memberships, we need one more ingredient, which is the baseline intensity of connections between nodes in block a and block b. This is given by the symmetric \(k \times k\) matrix \(B\). Then each edge \(A_{ij}\) is Poisson distributed with parameter

$$ \lambda_{ij} = z_i^T B z_j = \sum_{a = 1}^k \sum_{b = 1}^k Z_{ia} Z_{jb} B_{ab}. $$

That is, every pair of blocks \((a, b)\) with \(i\) in block \(a\) and \(j\) in block \(b\) contributes \(B_{ab}\) to the expected number of edges between \(i\) and \(j\), so two nodes that share more blocks connect at a higher rate. When expected_degree or expected_density is specified, \(B\) is multiplied by a constant to achieve the desired value, so only the relative magnitudes of the entries of \(B\) matter in that case.

In the factor model parameterization, the latent positions are \(X = Z\) and the mixing matrix \(S\) is the symmetrized and rescaled \(B\), so that \(\mathbb{E}[A \mid Z] = Z S Z^T\).

When poisson_edges = FALSE, the symmetrized and rescaled \(B\) is instead treated as a matrix of Bernoulli probabilities, and replaced by \(-\log(1 - B)\) (elementwise) before sampling. Nodes \(i\) and \(j\) are then connected with probability

$$ 1 - \prod_{a = 1}^k \prod_{b = 1}^k (1 - B_{ab})^{Z_{ia} Z_{jb}}, $$

that is, each pair of shared blocks independently gets a chance to connect \(i\) and \(j\). This is the "noisy-OR" model discussed in Section 3 of Kaufmann, Bonald and Lelarge (2016), and for sparse graphs it is close to the SBMO with Bernoulli edges.

Identifiability

Kaufmann, Bonald and Lelarge (2016, Theorem 1) show that the parameters \(k\), \(B\) and \(Z\) of an SBMO are identifiable, up to a permutation of the block labels, when:

  1. \(B\) is invertible, and

  2. there is at least one "pure node" in each block that belongs to no other blocks.

overlapping_sbm() checks that the symmetrized and rescaled \(B\) (i.e. S) is invertible, and force_pure = TRUE guarantees the second condition. Kaufmann, Bonald and Lelarge (2016) further assume that every node belongs to at least one block, which overlapping_sbm() guarantees by reassigning nodes that join no block (see "Block memberships" above).

Related models

Latouche, Birmelé and Ambroise (2011) introduced the overlapping stochastic block model (OSBM), which also uses binary membership vectors but passes them through a logistic link, so that block contributions add up on the logit scale rather than on the scale of the edge rate. The OSBM is not implemented in fastRG.

The overlapping continuous community assignment model (OCCAM) of Zhang, Levina and Zhu (2020) generalizes the SBMO by allowing non-negative, real-valued membership vectors (normalized to have unit length) and per-node degree heterogeneity parameters \(\theta_i\), with \(\mathbb{E}[A \mid Z, \theta] = \Theta Z B Z^T \Theta\) for \(\Theta = \mathrm{diag}(\theta)\). The SBMO can be viewed as a special case of the OCCAM (Kaufmann, Bonald and Lelarge 2016). overlapping_sbm() does not include degree heterogeneity parameters.

References

Kaufmann, Emilie, Thomas Bonald, and Marc Lelarge. 2016. "A Spectral Algorithm with Additive Clustering for the Recovery of Overlapping Communities in Networks." In Algorithmic Learning Theory (ALT 2016), edited by R. Ortner et al., 355–70. Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 9925. Cham: Springer International Publishing. doi:10.1007/978-3-319-46379-7_24 .

Latouche, Pierre, Etienne Birmelé, and Christophe Ambroise. 2011. "Overlapping Stochastic Block Models with Application to the French Political Blogosphere." The Annals of Applied Statistics 5 (1): 309–36. doi:10.1214/10-AOAS382 .

Zhang, Yuan, Elizaveta Levina, and Ji Zhu. 2020. "Detecting Overlapping Communities in Networks Using Spectral Methods." SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science 2 (2): 265–83. doi:10.1137/19M1272238 . Preprint: https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.3432.

Examples


set.seed(27)

lazy_overlapping_sbm <- overlapping_sbm(n = 1000, k = 5, expected_density = 0.01)
#> Setting `B` to a matrix with value 0.8 on the diagonal and 0.1 / (k - 1) on the off-diagonal. This parameterization may change in the future. Explicitly set `B` for reproducible results.
lazy_overlapping_sbm
#> Undirected Overlapping Stochastic Blockmodel
#> --------------------------------------------
#> 
#> Nodes (n): 1000 (sorted)
#> Blocks (k): 5
#> 
#> Traditional Overlapping SBM parameterization:
#> 
#> Block memberships (Z): 1000 x 5 [dgCMatrix] 
#> Block probabilities (pi): 5 [numeric] 
#> 
#> Block connection propensities (B): 5 x 5 [matrix] 
#> 
#> Factor model parameterization:
#> 
#> X: 1000 x 5 [dgCMatrix] 
#> S: 5 x 5 [dsyMatrix] 
#> 
#> Poisson edges: TRUE 
#> Allow self loops: TRUE 
#> 
#> Expected edges: 4995
#> Expected degree: 5
#> Expected density: 0.01

# block memberships: a binary matrix, nodes can belong to several blocks
lazy_overlapping_sbm$Z[1:5, ]
#> 5 x 5 sparse Matrix of class "dgCMatrix"
#>      block1 block2 block3 block4 block5
#> [1,]      1      1      1      1      .
#> [2,]      1      1      1      1      .
#> [3,]      1      1      1      .      1
#> [4,]      1      1      1      .      .
#> [5,]      1      1      1      .      .

# how many blocks does each node belong to? every node belongs to
# at least one block
table(Matrix::rowSums(lazy_overlapping_sbm$Z))
#> 
#>   1   2   3   4 
#> 734 186  74   6 

# sometimes you gotta let the world burn and
# sample a wildly dense graph

dense_lazy_overlapping_sbm <- overlapping_sbm(n = 500, k = 3, expected_density = 0.8)
#> Setting `B` to a matrix with value 0.8 on the diagonal and 0.1 / (k - 1) on the off-diagonal. This parameterization may change in the future. Explicitly set `B` for reproducible results.
dense_lazy_overlapping_sbm
#> Undirected Overlapping Stochastic Blockmodel
#> --------------------------------------------
#> 
#> Nodes (n): 500 (sorted)
#> Blocks (k): 3
#> 
#> Traditional Overlapping SBM parameterization:
#> 
#> Block memberships (Z): 500 x 3 [dgCMatrix] 
#> Block probabilities (pi): 3 [numeric] 
#> 
#> Block connection propensities (B): 3 x 3 [matrix] 
#> 
#> Factor model parameterization:
#> 
#> X: 500 x 3 [dgCMatrix] 
#> S: 3 x 3 [dsyMatrix] 
#> 
#> Poisson edges: TRUE 
#> Allow self loops: TRUE 
#> 
#> Expected edges: 99800
#> Expected degree: 199.6
#> Expected density: 0.8

# explicitly setting the mixing matrix and block membership
# probabilities rather than using defaults. pi does not need to
# sum to one: here nodes belong to 1.7 blocks on average

k <- 5
n <- 1000
B <- matrix(stats::runif(k * k), nrow = k, ncol = k)

pi <- c(1, 2, 4, 1, 0.5) / 5

custom_overlapping_sbm <- overlapping_sbm(
  n = n,
  B = B,
  pi = pi,
  expected_degree = 5
)

custom_overlapping_sbm
#> Undirected Overlapping Stochastic Blockmodel
#> --------------------------------------------
#> 
#> Nodes (n): 1000 (sorted)
#> Blocks (k): 5
#> 
#> Traditional Overlapping SBM parameterization:
#> 
#> Block memberships (Z): 1000 x 5 [dgCMatrix] 
#> Block probabilities (pi): 5 [numeric] 
#> 
#> Block connection propensities (B): 5 x 5 [matrix] 
#> 
#> Factor model parameterization:
#> 
#> X: 1000 x 5 [dgCMatrix] 
#> S: 5 x 5 [dgeMatrix] 
#> 
#> Poisson edges: TRUE 
#> Allow self loops: TRUE 
#> 
#> Expected edges: 5000
#> Expected degree: 5
#> Expected density: 0.01001

# pi is sorted, and B is permuted to match
custom_overlapping_sbm$pi
#> [1] 0.1 0.2 0.2 0.4 0.8
colMeans(custom_overlapping_sbm$Z)
#> block1 block2 block3 block4 block5 
#>  0.099  0.215  0.211  0.394  0.843 

edgelist <- sample_edgelist(custom_overlapping_sbm)
edgelist
#> # A tibble: 2,458 × 2
#>     from    to
#>    <int> <int>
#>  1     7    82
#>  2    24    46
#>  3     6    79
#>  4    55    97
#>  5     7    11
#>  6    22    79
#>  7     4    42
#>  8    27    72
#>  9     8    10
#> 10    15    55
#> # ℹ 2,448 more rows

A <- sample_sparse(custom_overlapping_sbm)

# nodes that belong to more blocks have higher degree on average
memberships <- Matrix::rowSums(custom_overlapping_sbm$Z)
tapply(Matrix::rowSums(A), memberships, mean)
#>         1         2         3         4 
#>  2.853488  5.752525  8.724359 11.222222 

# efficient eigendecompostion that leverages low-rank structure in
# E(A) so that you don't have to form E(A) to find eigenvectors,
# as E(A) is typically dense. computation is
# handled via RSpectra

population_eigs <- eigs_sym(custom_overlapping_sbm)
population_eigs$values
#> [1]  5.94938526  0.31139205  0.10099027  0.06603763 -0.31278692
